fatal_errors: The proposed grain-boundary precipitation treatment does not reconstruct the demonstrated Co-for-Ni substitution intervention.
No treatment temperature, hold time, cooling rate, magnetic field, pressure, operating-temperature interval, or mechanical-loading range is specified.

The claim that caloric performance will remain within 10% is unsupported and conflicts with the target evidence that mechanical improvement through increased Co content progressively reduces the first-order caloric response, with x = 0.55 showing only 2.6 J kg−1 K−1 at 5 T.

The cited evidence concerns an additive-containing high-entropy metal-diboride ceramic processed near 3000 K, not a Mn-Ni-Si-Fe-Co-Ge magnetocaloric alloy or preservation of a magnetostructural transition.
Pressure-caloric behavior is asserted without supporting evidence or a defined pressure protocol.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad engineering objective and supplies quantitative falsification thresholds, but it is not supported for this alloy and does not match the hidden study. The target intervention was systematic Co substitution for Ni from x = 0.40 to 0.55 after defined annealing and quenching. Its mechanism involved stabilization of the hexagonal Ni2In-type phase, downward shifts of structural and Curie transitions, and eventual loss of first-order magnetostructural coupling. Mechanical properties generally improved, but the giant magnetocaloric response was not preserved at the strongest composition: hardness reached 758 HV2 and compressive strength 267 MPa at x = 0.55 while peak entropy change fell to 2.6 J kg−1 K−1. The proposed precipitation mechanism may be generically plausible, but no evidence establishes that suitable coherent precipitates exist in this chemistry or that they leave transformation thermodynamics unchanged. The control experiment is directionally useful, yet insufficiently reproducible because all decisive processing and operating boundaries are left unspecified.
